authority: United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) / U.S. Code Title 35
title: 35 U.S.C. § 101 - Inventions Patentable
text: 35 U.S.C. 101 Inventions patentable: Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title. Under the Alice/Mayo framework, laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas are patent-ineligible. Natural botanical extracts and raw herbal compositions in an unmodified or naturally occurring state are ineligible under Section 101 unless marked differences in characteristics or non-natural synergistic combinations are created.

authority: United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) / Leahy-Smith America Invents Act (AIA)
title: 35 U.S.C. § 102 - Conditions for Patentability; Novelty
text: 35 U.S.C. 102 Conditions for patentability; novelty: (a) NOVELTY; PRIOR ART.—A person shall be entitled to a patent unless— (1) the claimed invention was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public before the effective filing date of the claimed invention; or (2) the claimed invention was described in a patent issued under section 151, or in an application for patent published or deemed published under section 122(b). Novelty requires that every element of the claimed invention must not have been disclosed in a single prior art reference prior to the effective filing date.

authority: United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) / 35 U.S.C.
title: 35 U.S.C. § 103 - Conditions for Patentability; Non-Obvious Subject Matter
text: 35 U.S.C. 103 Conditions for patentability; non-obvious subject matter: A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA) to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made. For herbal and botanical formulations, combining known active extracts is obvious unless unexpected synergistic results or technical advance is experimentally proven.

authority: United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) / 35 U.S.C.
title: 35 U.S.C. § 112 - Specification, Enablement, and Claim Requirements
text: 35 U.S.C. 112 Specification: (a) IN GENERAL.—The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor. (b) CONCLUSION.—The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor regards as the invention.

authority: United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) / 35 U.S.C.
title: 35 U.S.C. § 271 - Infringement of Patent and Territorial Monopoly Principle
text: 35 U.S.C. 271 Infringement of patent: (a) Except as otherwise provided in this title, whoever without authority makes, uses, offers to sell, or sells any patented invention, within the United States or imports into the United States any patented invention during the term of the patent therefor, infringes the patent. Patent rights are strictly territorial. A foreign patent (such as an Indian patent granted by the CGPDTM) grants no legal rights, commercial exclusivity, or defensive infringement protection in the United States.

authority: United States Food and Drug Administration (US FDA) / Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act
title: FD&C Act § 201(ff) [21 U.S.C. § 321(ff)] - Definition of Dietary Supplement under DSHEA
text: Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) Section 201(ff), codified at 21 U.S.C. § 321(ff), enacted by the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994 (DSHEA, Public Law 103-417): Defines a dietary supplement as a product (other than tobacco) intended to supplement the diet that contains one or more dietary ingredients, including a vitamin, mineral, herb or other botanical, amino acid, or dietary substance for use by man to supplement the diet by increasing total dietary intake. Dietary supplements are regulated as food under CFSAN, not as pharmaceutical drugs.

authority: United States Food and Drug Administration (US FDA) / 21 U.S.C.
title: FD&C Act § 403(r)(6) [21 U.S.C. § 343(r)(6)] - Dietary Supplement Claims & FDA Disclaimer
text: 21 U.S.C. 343(r)(6) Permitted Structure/Function Claims: A statement for a dietary supplement may claim a benefit related to a classical nutrient deficiency disease, describe the role of a nutrient intended to affect structure or function, or characterize documented mechanism of action, provided that the label prominently bears the mandatory FDA disclaimer: 'This statement has not been evaluated by the Food and Drug Administration. This product is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease.' Claims to diagnose, treat, prevent, or cure any disease convert the product into an unapproved new drug under 21 U.S.C. § 355.

authority: United States Food and Drug Administration (US FDA) / Code of Federal Regulations
title: 21 CFR Part 111 - Current Good Manufacturing Practice (cGMP) in Dietary Supplements
text: 21 CFR Part 111 Current Good Manufacturing Practice (cGMP) for Dietary Supplements: Mandates comprehensive quality control procedures, specifications for raw botanical components, identity testing for 100% of incoming botanical ingredients, in-process production controls, finished product testing against heavy metals (Lead, Arsenic, Cadmium, Mercury) and microbiological contamination, and master manufacturing record auditing.

authority: United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) / Trademark Act of 1946 (Lanham Act)
title: Lanham Act § 2(e)(1) [15 U.S.C. § 1052(e)(1)] - Refusal of Merely Descriptive or Generic Marks
text: 15 U.S.C. 1052(e)(1) Section 2: No trademark by which the goods of the applicant may be distinguished from the goods of others shall be refused registration on the principal register on account of its nature unless it consists of a mark which, (1) when used on or in connection with the goods of the applicant is merely descriptive or deceptively misdescriptive of them. Under established USPTO trademark examination practice (TMEP § 1209), common or generic botanical plant names, including Ayurvedic herbs such as 'Ashwagandha', 'Turmeric', 'Brahmi', or 'Triphala', cannot be registered on the Principal Register as exclusive trademarks for herbal teas, supplements, or dietary products because they merely describe an ingredient or genus of goods.

authority: United States Food and Drug Administration (US FDA CFSAN) / FD&C Act
title: FD&C Act § 413 [21 U.S.C. § 350b] - New Dietary Ingredient (NDI) 75-Day Premarket Notification
text: 21 U.S.C. 350b New Dietary Ingredients: A dietary supplement which contains a new dietary ingredient (an ingredient not marketed in the United States before October 15, 1994) shall be deemed adulterated unless the manufacturer or distributor submits a notification to the FDA at least 75 days before introducing the product into interstate commerce. The 75-day NDI notification must include documentation establishing that the dietary supplement will reasonably be expected to be safe under the conditions of use recommended in labeling.

authority: United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) / Code of Federal Regulations
title: 37 CFR § 1.321 & MPEP § 804 - Terminal Disclaimer to Obviate Double Patenting
text: 37 CFR 1.321 Statutory and Terminal Disclaimers: A terminal disclaimer is an official instrument filed by a patent owner or applicant to disclaim or dedicate to the public the entire term, or all terminal days of the term, of a patent. In patent prosecution involving botanical or pharmaceutical formulations, a terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321(c) is utilized to overcome a nonstatutory (obviousness-type) double patenting rejection by binding the patent to expire simultaneously with the reference patent and requiring common ownership throughout the enforceable term.

authority: United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) / 35 U.S.C.
title: 35 U.S.C. § 154 - Patent Term and Priority Calculation
text: 35 U.S.C. 154 Contents and term of patent: Subject to the payment of maintenance fees, a patent grant confers exclusive rights beginning on the date on which the patent issues and ending 20 years from the date on which the application for the patent was filed in the United States or, if the application contains a specific reference to an earlier filed application under section 120, 121, 365(c), or 386(c), from the date on which the earliest such application was filed. Patent Term Adjustment (PTA) under § 154(b) compensates for administrative USPTO examination delays.
